title: Russian strike on buses kills 33, say officials, as deadly attacks on Ukraine surge
content: Thirty-three people have been killed in a Russian glide bomb attack on two civilian buses in the frontline city of Kramatorsk, rescue officials say. Another 18 people were wounded, said Donetsk regional head Vadym Filashkin, accusing Russia of targeting buses carrying passengers to kill as many civilians as possible. Images posted by local prosecutors showed the burning metal shell of the bus along with debris and some of the victims on the road. Kramatorsk and neighbouring Slovyansk are part of a so-called fortress belt that Russia is trying to seize as part of Vladimir Putin's claim to the entire Ukrainian industrial region of Donbas. However, Thursday's attack follows a dramatic surge in Russian attacks across the country and a heavy increase in civilian casualties. According to the UN, Ukraine saw more civilians killed by August this year than were killed in all of 2025. In one single attack that destroyed a five-storey block of flats in Pryluky east of Kyiv early on Wednesday, 22 people were killed, including five children. Three of the children were only one year old. Moscow is yet to comment on the latest attack, however rescue officials said the attack caused a fire on two buses that were both carrying passengers. Filashkin appealed to anyone who was still in the Donetsk region to move to safer regions of Ukraine. Given the sharp deterioration of security in the two neighbouring cities, he said all public transport had been ordered to stop. The safety of civilians was paramount, and "we have no right to risk the lives of passengers and drivers", he said. Moscow has often cited the "liberation" and "protection" of the predominantly Russian-speaking Donbas as justification for the full-scale invasion of Ukraine. It is made up of two regions - Luhansk and Donetsk - and with most of Luhansk under Russian control, the Kremlin is also aiming to capture remaining 20% of Donetsk territory still held by Ukraine. Russia is also launching constant air raids on the capital Kyiv, with sirens ringing throughout the day. Kyiv's mayor Vitali Klitschko said attacks on Thursday had killed three people, with 14 others injured. Two of the eight injured are in a critical condition. The attacks are forcing schoolchildren out of classes into shelters, shuttering businesses, and disrupting public transport. Russian attacks on Ukrainian infrastructure, particularly on its energy grid, are causing power outages already and are even affecting the water supply. Local water authorities in the capital warned on Thursday that pressure was dropping across the city's right bank due to power cuts. Zelensky offered his condolences to families and loved ones affected by the latest attack and said Ukraine's partners needed to provide "concrete action through new defence packages for the protection of Ukraine". Ahead of the Pryluky attack, the Ukrainian leader had warned this week of warned of intelligence suggesting plans for a major Russian onslaught, and in Kyiv families responded by heading to metro stations for shelter. Such warnings are for now one of the only defences Ukrainians have. Interceptor missiles are in short supply around the world, so Ukraine has little chance to stop incoming Russian ballistics. Both Russia and Ukraine have intensified long-range strikes on each other in recent months, with Russian attacks targeting Ukrainian data centres and logistics warehouses. For much of the war Kramatorsk acted as a logistics and supply hub for the Ukrainian military, however it has now come under almost daily Russian attack as its military moves closer to the east of the city. Glide bombs in particular have been launched at Slovyansk and Kramatorsk. The bombs are fitted with winglets so they glide towards their target rather than simply fall. In late August as many as nine glide bombs were fired at Kramatorsk in one day. Kramatorsk City Council described the strike as a "horrific crime committed by the Russian army against the civilian population". "Once again, the Russians have struck a location where there are absolutely no military targets." The club's chair praises people's "phenomenal" generosity, which he says "makes it all worthwhile". Fears that the death may have been caused by pneumonic plague has prompted calls for more transparency from Russia. The death of a worker from a Russian lab that researches plague has prompted questions about the disease. The World Health Organization said Russian authorities had identified all of the people who had been in contact with a laboratory worker. The US and Russia have each offered to help each other tackling infectious diseases. Copyright 2026 BBC. All rights reserved. The BBC is not responsible for the content of external sites. ranking_reason: A devastating Russian attack on civilian buses in Ukraine has resulted in a significant loss of human life and a surge in attacks across the country, highlighting the urgent need for international action to protect civilians and prevent further violence.

title: Could Christa Pike face execution again and by what method?
content: The botched execution of Tennessee death row inmate Christa Pike has thrust Tennessee's criminal justice system into uncharted territory. A week after receiving two lethal doses of the drug pentobarbital, she is said to be walking and talking again in limited ways. Tennessee Governor Bill Lee has ordered an independent investigation and suspended all executions for the rest of the year. The fate of Pike, who has been on death row for 30 years for murdering Colleen Slemmer, now lies in a mysterious grey area. At a hearing on Wednesday, an attorney for Tennessee said the decision on scheduling a new execution date was up to the state's supreme court. But Pike's lawyers are seeking to have her death sentence commuted to life in prison without parole. Lee, who has commutation powers, has not indicated what the state will do. Slemmer was murdered by both Pike and Pike's then-boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, who was not an adult at the time so was spared the death penalty and remains in prison. The BBC spoke to multiple experts to explore what could happen next. The Tennessee Department of Correction could attempt to execute Pike again by lethal injection, but the state would very likely run into legal challenges based on constitutional protections against cruel and unusual punishment. "For the state to attempt to execute her again using the same methodology, they would have severe legal hurdles," Tennessee-based defence attorney Stephen Ross Johnson said. Johnson said Tennessee had botched two executions in one year - it also failed to kill Tony Carruthers in May - which could give lawyers the grounds to argue broadly against the constitutionality of the state’s lethal injection protocol. Pike's lawyers could also argue a lethal injection is what Johnson called "unconstitutional as applied", meaning it is cruel and unusual specifically for Pike, due to her medical condition. Pike's lawyers had warned before the execution attempt that she has small veins and thrombocytosis, a blood-clotting condition that would complicate the procedure. Her medical condition combined with the state's botched execution would make it difficult for Tennessee to present a convincing legal argument for attempting lethal injection again, Johnson said. Johnson, president-elect of the National Association of Criminal Defense Lawyers, could see the state attempting an execution by a different method. This would require "additional legal hoops", including approval from the governor's office and potentially the state legislature. Since Pike's survival, political leaders in Tennessee have called for moving her death sentence forward through other means. Senator Marsha Blackburn, the Republican candidate for governor in next month's election, said: "Bring back the electric chair." Congressman Tim Burchett, posted on social media that he's already filed a bill to "bring back hanging". Tennessee could be allowed to use the electric chair because Pike committed the murder in 1995 before the state changed its execution laws. She would need to waive her right to lethal injection in writing, which means it would have to be her decision, Vanderbilt University law professor Chris Slobogin said. Given that Pike's exact medical state is unknown, Slobogin said there was a scenario in which the state could be blocked from attempting to execute her again, regardless of method. It was also considered cruel and unusual punishment to execute someone who is mentally incapable of understanding why it is happening, he explained. Historically this has applied to prisoners with dementia or psychosis, but experts have said there is a chance that Pike has suffered brain damage. There is a precedent of states finding a different method to execute a death-row inmate. In 2024, Alabama executed a convicted murderer using a different method to the one that was originally planned. Kenneth Eugene Smith was put to death using nitrogen gas - having failed with its initial plan of lethal injection. Tennessee is taking a long pause on carrying out capital punishment. Only one person was due to be executed this year after Pike, which the governor has now postponed. Earlier, in May, the Carruthers execution was suspended by a year after state officials could not find a vein to administer the lethal injection - meaning that he has a year-long reprieve. It will therefore probably take a while for any movement in Pike's case. "At a minimum there's going to be some significant delay while this issue is studied by the state", defence attorney Johnson said, adding Pike's health would also need to be studied. Slobogin suspects the governor will commute her sentence, especially if missteps by state officials are uncovered in the investigation he has ordered. "If the investigation, in any way, shape, or form, suggests that the protocol was not followed, or is hard to carry out, that might be the easy way for him to go, given the complications with the execution and all the bad press," he said. There is legal precedent for a death sentence to be commuted due to a botched execution combined with an inmate's poor medical state. The execution of Alabama death-row prisoner Doyle Hamm was called off after more than two hours of attempts to establish an IV line failed. The state gave up on executing him following a legal settlement that related, in part, to his health. He later died of natural causes. Lawyers for Jamaal Howard had asked a judge to pause the execution after Christa Pike's botched lethal injections. The US death row inmate's legal team said at a press conference that she is now "conscious and speaking" after her failed execution. A medical expert advising her legal team says the murderer of Colleen Slemmer is communicating in a "basic way". Nidal Malik Hasan killed 13 unarmed soldiers and injured another 32 in the deadliest ever non-combat attack on an American military base. The BBC's Sarah Smith details the injuries sustained by the US death row inmate after two failed lethal injections, and what comes next. Copyright 2026 BBC. All rights reserved. title: Spanish pensioner whose eviction sparked nationwide protests dies
content: An elderly woman whose eviction sparked nationwide protests over Spain's housing crisis and a political row that triggered early elections has died, according to Madrid's tenants union. Maricarmen Abascal, 87, was forcibly removed on a stretcher from her apartment of more than 70 years on 23 September after she was unable to afford steep rent increases. The company that owned the flat later offered to allow her to return at a lower rate - but she was unable to sign an agreement as she had been admitted to hospital. Announcing her death, Madrid Tenants' Union said Abascal's situation marked "a turning point in the history of this country". The 87-year-old and her eviction became a symbol for Spain's housing crisis. The Socialist-led government sought to respond to the protests but its bid to push through urgent housing measures failed, prompting Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez to call snap elections. "Speculation costs lives, and today rent profiteering has finished killing our colleague Maricarmen," said union spokeswoman Alicia del Río. "Her memory lives on and makes us fight even harder." The 87-year-old was already in fragile health at the time of her eviction and she was admitted to Madrid's Gregorio Marañón Hospital, sending messages of support to protesters from her hospital bed. When news of her death reached Puerta del Sol - the Madrid square where thousands have camped since her eviction to demand more affordable housing - there was a collective gasp, followed by a minute of silence. Dozens of candles were lit around the square, with more laid out to form an altar to Abascal in front of the headquarters of the Community of Madrid government. Messages laid at the scene read "it's not a death, it's a killing", "the fight will continue" and "Maricarmen, the grandmother of the whole country", among others. Maricarmen Abascal's father had first rented the flat in Madrid's Retiro district in 1956 and she continued as the tenant after her parents died, during which time there was a cap on the rent. The area has become increasingly sought-after, and Urbagestión, the company that bought the property in 2018, increased the rent from €500 per month (£428; $572) to €2,650 (£2,280; $3,020). Rental costs in Madrid have soared by more than 100% over the last decade, according to property site Idealista. The company later offered to reduce this to €1,650 - still €300 more than Abascal's monthly pension. Three earlier attempts to evict her had been blocked by the courts and her case attracted widespread support from the public and celebrities. Prime Minister Sánchez's minority government announced two emergency decrees to tackle the housing crisis, but they were rejected in Congress last week , and on Monday he called elections for 29 November. Opponents pointed out he had had eight years in office to respond to the issue. Tens of thousands of people took to the streets last weekend in cities across the country, as protests continued. "All my love goes to Maricarmen's family and loved ones," Sánchez said on Wednesday night. "A hug as well to everyone who today feels this loss as their own." The leader of the opposition People's Party, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, also sent his condolences, appealing for her death not to be politicised: "No campaign, no parties, no self-interested exploitation. No more stones in the wall. "In the face of a person's death, only respect is in order," he added. The Madrid Tenants' Union said the events surrounding her eviction represented a turning point in the country's history, but added that the cost to get to this point had been "too high". In one video recorded from her hospital bed following her eviction, Maricarmen said: "I haven't managed to defend my home, but I have fought so that others can learn to fight for what's theirs." A few hundred people marched from Puerta del Sol to parliament on Wednesday night, chanting "we will not tolerate a single eviction more" and "the fight will continue, Maricarmen is still alive". There were other chants against the police. Many protesters believed that police had been complicit in the evictions, as under court orders they have to remove tenants who have been served eviction notices. After a couple of hours, the chants near Congress gave way to another minute of silence. Then, a big collective shout of "murderers". One protester told the BBC that people would remain in the square "as long as necessary". Earlier on Wednesday, unions had called a general strike to take place on 11 November, demanding housing reforms. The public outcry over Abascal's situation exposed the deep political divisions in Spain. The political right argued that the government's attempt to intervene in the housing market would have led to fewer homes being rented and would have raised prices further. Sánchez said on Monday he needed "a broader progressive majority" that could "overcome the resistance of the elites" to push through reforms. However, other issues unrelated to housing, including numerous corruption scandals linked to his party, and pressures relating to the cost of living and immigration, have also caused him problems. Most opinion polls suggest the conservative People's Party is likely to emerge as the largest party in the next election. However, they would be expected to need the support of the hard-right Vox party, currently third in the polls, to form a government. Additional reporting by Tom McArthur Copyright 2026 BBC. ranking_reason: The public should care because this event represents a turning point in Spain's housing crisis, with major implications for the country's politics and economy.
